concepts.title: Python, data and tests
concepts.prove: Write a tokenizer and a word counter, then pass unseen tests without copying a solution.
concepts.reuse: Keep your tokenizer, dataset loader and test helpers. Every later project needs these.
concepts.tools: Python standard library; existing Practice exercises

concepts.title: Vectors, gradients and learning
concepts.prove: Explain tensor shapes, compute a numerical gradient check, and train a tiny network on held-out data.
concepts.reuse: One reproducible training loop, seed setup, metrics function and dataset split.
concepts.tools: NumPy and PyTorch locally; use the existing exercises first

concepts.title: Transformers and local inference
concepts.prove: Explain attention, tokens, context and KV cache. Measure latency and memory on one small local model.
concepts.reuse: A single model adapter with timeouts and a fixed evaluation set. Change models behind that interface.
concepts.tools: Ollama optional; begin with an already installed small local model

concepts.title: Retrieval with evidence
concepts.prove: Build ten answerable and five unanswerable questions; measure retrieval recall and inspect each answer's citations.
concepts.reuse: Stable source IDs, content hashes, chunking and your question set. Start with this app's BM25 search.
concepts.tools: Built-in BM25; optional local embeddings and Qdrant after measurement

concepts.title: Bounded agents and tool contracts
concepts.prove: Validate a tool call's schema, enforce a three-step budget, and require approval before a write. Test a malicious retrieved instruction.
concepts.reuse: Tool schemas, a read-only retriever, a trace format, and a state object. Add orchestration only when the workflow needs it.
concepts.tools: Plain functions first; LangGraph for persisted workflows; MCP for interoperable tools

concepts.title: Adapt a model when evidence justifies it
concepts.prove: Compare prompts and RAG against a small LoRA experiment on a held-out task. Keep training and evaluation data separate.
concepts.reuse: Versioned datasets and the same evaluation harness used before tuning.

concepts.title: Evaluation, observability and reuse
concepts.prove: Record quality, latency, failure cases and model/version for every run. Replay your test set before replacing a component.
concepts.reuse: A component registry: purpose, interface, data version, test result, failure modes and next step.
concepts.tools: JSONL traces and local tests; optional OpenTelemetry later

concepts.prove: Read and search offline on Android; play exported audio with the screen locked; time inference only on hardware that fits.
concepts.reuse: The same static course and audio files across Android, laptop and an optional Pi file server.

episodes.title: Build once. Learn in layers.
episodes.summary: A reusable path from your first tokenizer to a grounded AI assistant.
episodes.text: Welcome to LLM From Zero. This is a short listening lesson about making each project help the next one. Imagine building a toolbox. The first project is a word counter. It teaches you to open a file, split text and count values. The next project is a tokenizer. It reuses the file reader and the tests. Later, retrieval reuses those same pieces to find useful passages. You are adding tools to one box instead of buying a new box every week. Here is a useful rule: learn a small idea by implementing it once, then use a maintained library when the real project grows. Writing a tiny vector similarity function teaches geometry. Maintaining your own production vector database usually does not help your learning goal. Keep a record for each component: what problem it solves, its inputs, its outputs, one working example, a test, and its limits. That record is your reuse notebook. When a new framework appears, ask which interface it would replace and which measured problem it solves. A new name is not enough. Your learning path has three activities. Listen for the explanation on your phone. Explain the idea from memory when you are parked. Then build and test it on the laptop. Listening is useful familiarity, but it is not proof that you can implement something. That is why the roadmap asks for evidence before you mark a concept verified. Think of a skill you have already learned. What small artifact would prove it, and where would you reuse that artifact? Keep that question in mind. The next time you build, start from the artifact you already trust.

episodes.title: What a language model actually does
episodes.summary: Tokens, context, generation and why a convincing answer can still be wrong.
episodes.text: A language model predicts tokens. A token may be a word, part of a word, punctuation or another text fragment. During training, the model adjusts numbers called weights so that useful continuations become more likely. During inference, those weights stay fixed while the model generates tokens. Think of context as the papers laid out on a desk. The model can use what is on the desk for the current request, but adding a page to the desk does not retrain it. A longer context window lets you place more pages there. It also uses memory and computation, and it does not guarantee that every detail will be used correctly. Attention is a mechanism for mixing information from different positions. A transformer stacks attention and other transformations to turn token representations into predictions. At generation time, a cache can retain earlier attention keys and values so they need not be recomputed at each step. This is the KV cache. It speeds generation but grows with context. The next token can be selected greedily or sampled. Temperature changes how concentrated the probability distribution is. Lower temperature often makes output less varied. It does not turn an unreliable fact into a verified fact. Quantization stores model numbers with fewer bits. It can help a model fit on your laptop, with possible quality tradeoffs. Parameter count alone does not tell you actual runtime memory: context, cache and implementation also matter. On your ThinkPad, begin with a small installed model and measure response time and memory. The practical question is whether it answers your evaluation questions reliably enough. Remember three separate things: training changes weights, context supplies temporary information, and retrieval selects which information enters that context. How would you explain the difference between training a model and giving it a document?

episodes.title: RAG: an open-book answer
episodes.summary: Follow a question through chunks, retrieval, evidence and an answer.
episodes.text: Retrieval augmented generation is an open-book workflow. Instead of asking a model to answer only from its weights, you first find useful text and give that text to the model. Imagine asking a librarian a question. The librarian chooses a few relevant pages. Then a writer uses those pages to draft an answer. Retrieval is the librarian. Generation is the writer. A basic pipeline starts with documents. Each document needs a stable identity and a version. Split long documents into passages called chunks. Chunks that are too small may lose context. Chunks that are too large may dilute the useful part and use the model's context budget. Overlap can preserve continuity, but it also duplicates text. Start with a simple baseline and measure. Keyword search such as BM25 rewards matching terms, especially rarer terms. Embedding search maps text into vectors so that related meanings can be close even when words differ. Hybrid search combines signals. A reranker can examine the candidate passages more carefully. Each extra stage has a cost, so add one only when your question set shows a useful improvement. Retrieved evidence should carry a source title and a passage identifier. Ask the model to cite those identifiers. A citation is a claim of support, not proof of support: inspect whether the passage actually says what the answer claims. When there is no good evidence, the right answer may be that the sources do not answer the question. A dangerous failure happens when a document contains instructions such as ignore your rules. Retrieved text is data, not authority. The model should not treat document instructions as commands. This learning studio starts with keyword retrieval. It shows the exact passages even without a model, and it can pass those passages to an optional local model. What would you test first if an answer were wrong: the retrieved pages, the prompt, or the model? Inspect the pages first, because even a good writer cannot quote a page that the librarian never found.

episodes.title: Measure before adding another framework
episodes.summary: A small evaluation set makes progress visible and prevents repeated work.
episodes.text: An impressive demonstration is not an evaluation. A demonstration shows one example that works. An evaluation asks whether the system works across a deliberate set of examples, including failures. Start small. Write ten questions whose answers are in your documents and five questions whose answers are absent. Record the expected source for each answerable question. Keep these examples separate from examples you use to tune your prompts. First measure retrieval. Recall at k asks whether useful evidence appears in the first k results. Precision asks how many selected results are useful. Reciprocal rank rewards placing the first relevant result early. These measure retrieval, not the truth of the final answer. Then inspect generation. Is the answer supported by the retrieved passages? Does each citation point to the right evidence? Does the system abstain on an unanswerable question? Also record response time, model name, prompt version, chunking settings and document version. Now imagine changing from keyword search to embeddings. Run the same questions before and after the change. If semantic search improves paraphrase questions but misses exact model identifiers, hybrid search might be useful. If there is no measurable improvement, keep the simpler version. Evaluation also protects your future self from repeating experiments. Save the result and the decision in your reuse notebook. Record what failed, why it failed, and what you tried. A future project can begin from that evidence. Do not label a system production ready because a few tests pass. Your local question set is a useful regression check within its scope. It is not a universal quality certificate. What is one unanswerable question you would include in an evaluation of your own notes? That question is often more revealing than an easy success.

episodes.title: Agents: decisions inside boundaries
episodes.summary: Tools, state, budgets and why a predictable workflow is often enough.
episodes.text: A workflow follows steps you choose. An agent uses a model to choose some next steps. Both can call tools. The useful distinction is how much decision making you delegate. Imagine a research assistant who can search a shelf, read a page and draft a note. You may allow those three actions. You do not automatically allow the assistant to delete the shelf or email the note. A tool contract defines a tool name, its argument schema, the result and its permissions. Validate arguments outside the model. A plausible JSON object can still contain the wrong file path or an invalid amount. Keep state explicitly: the question, retrieved evidence, completed steps, errors and remaining budget. Set a limit on steps and time. Handle repeated tool calls and failed results. Stop if the assistant cannot make progress. A deterministic retrieve then answer workflow is often enough for a study application. Add planning only when the task requires choosing among different useful paths. LangGraph can help express long-running stateful workflows, including checkpoints and human review. It is an optional orchestration choice, not a requirement for every model call. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, provides a standard way for AI applications to connect to tools and resources. It helps reuse integrations. It does not make a connected tool safe by itself, and it does not guarantee that model decisions are correct. Trace what happened: which tool was called, what inputs were validated, what evidence came back and why execution stopped. Test a malicious instruction hidden inside a retrieved document. Test a timeout and a duplicate request. Keep write actions behind explicit human approval. What is the smallest set of read-only tools your learning assistant actually needs? Begin there and expand only when a real task requires it.

episodes.title: Your laptop, your phone and your Pi
episodes.summary: Give each device a useful role without paying for cloud infrastructure.
episodes.text: Your devices can share the learning work without sharing the same workload. The laptop is the workshop. Use it for coding, tests, indexing notes and running a local model when the available memory allows it. The Android phone is the reading and listening device. The Raspberry Pi can be a lightweight file or static web server if you want an always-on library. A Raspberry Pi 2 Model B has one gigabyte of RAM according to its official specification. If yours has two or four gigabytes, it may be a different model. On Raspberry Pi OS, checking the device model and memory will resolve that uncertainty. Do not plan a modern language model workload around an unverified board. For the ThinkPad, an Intel i7 describes the processor family but does not tell us total RAM or graphics memory. Check those before selecting a large model. Start small. A quantized model may fit in less memory, but its working memory also depends on context length and the runtime. A free local tool avoids per-call API charges; it still uses your electricity, storage and download bandwidth. Keep the phone experience independent of the laptop. Saved lessons should open offline after the app has cached them. Browser narration may stop when Android locks the screen or suspends the browser. For a journey, export audio files on Windows and copy them to your phone before leaving. Use a media player that supports background playback. Downloaded files make this much more dependable. Your progress in the original app and the studio use separate backups, so transfer each when needed. Automatic live synchronization is not included. One device builds, another presents, and files carry the work between them. Which task belongs on which device in your own routine?

episodes.title: Prompting, RAG or fine-tuning?
episodes.summary: Choose the intervention that matches the problem you observe.
episodes.text: Suppose your assistant gives weak answers. There are several possible reasons. The instruction may be unclear. The needed facts may be missing. The answer format may require a specialized skill. These are different problems. Begin with prompting when the model already has the capability and needs a clearer task, examples or output structure. Use retrieval when answers depend on documents or facts that you can provide. Retrieval makes the chosen evidence visible and lets you update documents without retraining model weights. Consider fine-tuning when you need to adapt behavior, style or task performance and you have appropriate examples. Fine-tuning changes learned parameters. It does not guarantee exact memory of every training fact. LoRA is a parameter-efficient approach that trains smaller adapter matrices rather than updating all model weights. It can reduce the resources needed for an adaptation experiment, but it still requires suitable hardware, data preparation and evaluation. Quantization and adapter training can be combined in some workflows, but the supported configuration depends on your libraries and model. Do not choose an experiment just because a laptop has a gaming label. Check memory and test the actual setup. Keep a held-out set. If you evaluate only on training examples, you may measure memorization rather than useful improvement. Compare a simple prompt, a retrieval baseline and the adaptation on the same task. Save the dataset version, settings, result and decision. You may discover that retrieval fixes the problem without tuning. Or that a smaller model with an adapter is more useful for a narrow task. The important result is the measured behavior. What evidence would convince you to train an adapter instead of improving retrieval?

episodes.title: A learning session that survives the commute
episodes.summary: Turn listening into recall, a small build and a reusable artifact.
episodes.text: Here is a learning rhythm for a busy day. Before the journey, choose one idea and prepare the audio while parked. Keep the lesson short enough to connect its beginning to its end. During the journey, focus on listening. Do not operate the learning app while driving. A good spoken lesson has an intuition, an example and one question to remember. It does not read a long code listing or a table of symbols aloud. After parking, answer that question in your own words before reopening the text. This exposes the difference between recognizing an explanation and being able to recall it. Later on the laptop, build one small thing that uses the idea. If you listened to retrieval, create three documents and rank them for a question. If you listened to agents, validate one tool call and reject an invalid one. If you listened to evaluation, add one answerable and one unanswerable question. Finish by saving an artifact and a note. The note should name the concept, describe the interface, link to the artifact, state the test result and record a next step. The original app's recall system can bring lessons back after a delay. Use it alongside this studio's notebook. Listening does not automatically mark a skill verified. Only mark it verified after you can explain and demonstrate it. On a short day, one paragraph from memory is still useful. On a longer day, a tested component can become the starting point for next week's project. Learning builds through these connections. What will you explain, build and save after today's lesson?
